Write a sample-size justification from a power result

Source: R/power_report.R
power_report.Rd

Turns the result of power_mixed(), power_design() or precision_design(), with the target_n() result that solved a curve for the sample size, into a sample-size justification in Markdown, ready for a preregistration, a registered report or a grant application.

Usage

power_report(
  x,
  solved = NULL,
  spec_file = NULL,
  justification = NULL,
  null_result = NULL,
  rope = NULL
)

# S3 method for class 'pilotr_report'
print(x, ...)

Arguments

x

For power_report(), the result of power_mixed(), power_design() or precision_design() at one design. A curve goes to target_n(), and its result to solved. For print(), a report.

solved

Optional result of target_n(), or of solve_curve() for an axis other than sample size, which gives the desired power and the value solved for it.

spec_file

Optional path of the specification file the analysis read. The report gives the MD5 checksum of its bytes, its seed and its units.

justification

Optional justification of each focal effect's size: one string for every focal effect, or a character vector named by focal effect. An effect without one is reported as having none.

null_result

Optional result of the same analysis with every focal effect set to zero. A result whose focal effects are not zero is refused.

rope

The region of practical equivalence given to precision_design(), as a half-width or an interval, which the report states. It applies to a precision result alone.

...

Ignored, present for consistency with the generic.

Value

A character string of class pilotr_report holding the Markdown, which ends in a newline. Printing it shows the text, and cat(report, file = "justification.md") saves it. The same arguments always give the same text.

Details

The sections follow the recommendations of Lakens (2022, Table 4) for reporting an a-priori power analysis. The primary analysis comes first, with its model, test, alpha and sidedness, then the desired power and the sample size solved for it, with its interval. Each focal effect follows, with its true value, the justification given for that value and its power. Last comes the power when the null hypothesis is true. The simulation is then accounted for as Morris, White and Crowther (2019) recommend for simulation studies: the replicates simulated and those that returned an estimate, the fits that were singular or carried a warning, and the Monte Carlo standard error of every rate. The report ends with what a reader needs to reproduce the run: the software and its versions, the specification's seed and an MD5 checksum of the specification file's bytes. The versions are those loaded when the report is written, so write it in the session that ran the analysis.

Each rate's Monte Carlo standard error and 95% Wilson interval are computed in the report from the number of significant replicates and the number of replicates behind the rate, with the functions that compute them in the results. Type S has its Wilson interval from the number of wrong signs among the significant replicates. The Python twin's power_report() writes the same text, byte for byte, from the same counts, which tools/parity/report_cross.py in the source repository checks.

The rates are those of the design x simulated. A sample size solved from a curve need not be that design's, so a justification usually pairs the solved size with a run of power_mixed() at that size. spec_file names the specification of that run, and the report lists its units. A result carries neither its specification nor its seed, so without spec_file the report says that both are missing.

null_result is the result of the same analysis of a design whose focal effects are all zero, such as the null condition that design_conditions() puts first. Its rejection rate is the Type I error rate of the test, which for a Wald z with few subjects or items can exceed alpha, and which a preregistered simplification rule can raise (see power_mixed()).

A precision_design() result gives a report on the interval and the region of practical equivalence in place of the test. Each focal effect then has its mean interval width, the probability of a meaningful effect, with the interval wholly outside the region, and the probability of practical equivalence, with the interval wholly inside it. rope states the region, since the result does not record it. A target_n() result solved over p_meaningful gives the desired probability of a meaningful decision. This section exists in R alone, as precision_design() does.

References

Lakens, D. (2022). Sample size justification. Collabra: Psychology, 8(1), 33267. doi:10.1525/collabra.33267

Morris, T. P., White, I. R. and Crowther, M. J. (2019). Using simulation studies to evaluate statistical methods. Statistics in Medicine, 38(11), 2074-2102. doi:10.1002/sim.8086

See also

target_n() for the sample size a curve implies, and design_conditions() for the null condition.

Examples

spec <- build_spec(list(name = "d", seed = 1, design_kind = "between",
  factor_name = "group", lev1 = "a", lev2 = "b", n_subject = 64,
  intercept = 100, effect = 5, family = "gaussian", resp_name = "", sigma = 10))
# n_sims is small so the example runs quickly. Use 200 or more for real planning.
res <- power_design(spec, n_sims = 50)
spec_file <- tempfile(fileext = ".json")
writeLines(spec_json(spec), spec_file)
power_report(res, spec_file = spec_file,
  justification = "Half a standard deviation, the smallest difference worth acting on.")
#> # Sample-size justification
#> 
#> ## Primary analysis
#> 
#> - Model and test: stats::t.test, two-sample t with pooled variance
#> - Significance level: alpha = 0.05, two-sided
#> - Simulated units: subject 64
#> 
#> ## Focal effects
#> 
#> The rates below are those of the simulated design, each over the replicates that returned an estimate for the effect.
#> 
#> ### The difference between the two groups
#> 
#> - True value: 5
#> - Justification: Half a standard deviation, the smallest difference worth acting on.
#> - Power: 0.520 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.071; 95% Wilson interval 0.385 to 0.652), from 26 of 50 replicates
#> - Type S: 0.000 (95% Wilson interval 0.000 to 0.129)
#> - Type M: 1.304 (Monte Carlo standard error 0.047)
#> 
#> ## Monte Carlo accounting
#> 
#> - Replicates: 50 simulated
#> 
#> Each rate's Monte Carlo standard error is sqrt(p(1 - p) / n), over the n replicates that returned an estimate, and its interval is the 95% Wilson score interval. The standard error of Type M is the standard deviation of the exaggeration ratios over the square root of their number.
#> 
#> ## Reproducibility
#> 
#> - Software: pilotr 0.3.1, R 4.6.1
#> - Specification: file19fa75d164f8.json, MD5 checksum fb7cf3e60def2bacdd2e7508dc1575be
#> - Seed: 1
